overview.body:
**Hēraklēs** ​(*herakles*) — ‌The Glory ‌of Labors ​— belongs ​to ​the Greek ​tradition, where ​it is ‌catalogued ​under the ​domain "Strength, ‌Labours, Heroism". ​The name ‌means ​"Glory of ‌Hera (from ​Ἥρα + ​κλέος)"[^1].

Hēraklēs ​is ​the **greatest ​of Greek ‌heroes** and ​the ‌only one ​to become ‌a full ​Olympian god. ‌His ​very name ‌means 'Glory ​of Hera,' ​yet ‌Hera persecuted ‌him from ‌the cradle, ​driving him ​to ‌madness and ​murder. His ​life is ‌a sequence ​of ​impossible tasks ‌performed under ​duress: the ‌Twelve ​Labours, the ​conquest of ​monsters, the ​rescue of ‌captives, ‌and finally ​a death ‌by fire ​that turned ​into ‌immortality.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ‌name as ‌**Hēraklēs** ​and serves ‌its temple ​at [hēraklēs.com](https://xn--hrakls-p3ae.com). ​The restoration ​preserves ‌vowel length ​— a ​description computed ​from ‌the displayed ​form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII form ‌*herakles* ​survives as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by the ​early ‌domain-name system; ‌the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Greek ​as ​**Ἡρακλῆς**. Etymologically ​it ​means "Glory ​of Hera ‌(from ​Ἥρα + ​κλέος)"[^1].

‌The ASCII ​form ‌*herakles* survives ​only ‌because the ​early ​domain-name system ​could ​not carry ​diacritics; ‌it is ​a technological ‌compromise, ​not an ‌ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode ​restoration **Hēraklēs** ‌recovers ​the vowel ​length ‌of the ‌original ‌directly in ​the ​address bar. ‌The restoration ​preserves ​vowel length ‌— ​a description ​computed ‌from the ​displayed ‌form itself.

​The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ​**h** → ‌**H** — ‌Rough ​breathing
- **e** ‌→ ​**ē** — ​Eta: ‌long epsilon
- ‌**r** ‌→ **r** ‌— ​Rho
- **a** ‌→ ​**a** — ​Short ​alpha
- **k** ‌→ **k** ​— ​Kappa
- **l** ​→ ‌**l** — ​Lambda
- ​**e** → ​**ē** ‌— Eta: ​long ‌epsilon
- **s** ​→ ‌**s** — ​Sigma

‌The project ‌holds the ​domain ​**hēraklēs.com** (xn--hrakls-p3ae.com) ​as ​the canonical ‌home ‌of this ​name[^2].

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name ‌is **/hɛː.ra.klɛ̂ːs/** — ​Classical Attic ​Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by phoneme:

- ​**Hē-** — ​Rough breathing ‌[h] plus long ​open-mid front ​eta [ɛː] ‌— the 'Hera' ​element, sustained ‌and deep.
- ​**-ra-** — Short ‌alpha with ​rolling alveolar ​rho, the link ​between the ​two halves ​of the name.
- ‌**-klēs** — ​Kappa-lambda followed ‌by long eta ​with circumflex ‌[klɛ̂ːs], carrying ​both length and ‌the falling ​pitch accent.

‌For the modern ​speaker, the ​closest approximation ‌is: "hay-RAH-KLAYS" — ‌first syllable ‌deeper and ​longer than English ​'hay'; the ‌final syllable ​is held and ​falls in ‌pitch, like ​'klays' sung on ​a descending ‌note.

Kindred ​and historical ‌forms of the ​name:

- **Greek** ​— Ἥρᾱ ​(Hḗrā), 'Hera'
- **Greek** ​— κλέος ‌(kléos), 'glory'
- ‌**Latin** — Herculēs, ​the Roman ‌adaptation via ​Etruscan hercle

Hēraklēs ​preserves both ‌features because ‌Classical Attic Ἡρακλῆς ‌contains both ‌length (long ​η in the ‌first and ​final syllables) ​and stress (circumflex ​on the ‌final -klēs). ​The registrable form ​Hēraklēs preserves ​length with ‌macrons; the acute/circumflex ​is omitted ​because fully ​accented Greek letters ‌are often ​untypeable and ‌are not reliably ​registrable as ‌IDN labels. ​Reconstruction follows Allen, ‌Vox Graeca: ‌The Pronunciation ​of Classical Greek, ​3rd ed. ​(Cambridge, 1987); ​LSJ; and Beekes, ‌Etymological Dictionary ‌of Greek ​(Brill, 2010).

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved in ‌Greek as ​**Ἡρακλῆς** — ​Greek alphabet ​(Classical / ​Attic), attested ​Ancient Greek, ‌c. 8th ​century ​BCE – ‌present, in ​Greece and ‌the Greek-speaking ​Mediterranean. The ‌script is ​written left-to-right.[^1]

​The scholarly ​transliteration is ​*Hēraklēs* ​(Greek alphabet ‌with polytonic ​accents), giving ‌the normalized ​reading /hɛːˈra.klɛːs/.

‌The rendering ​proceeds step ‌by step:

- ​The ‌Greek form ​Ἡρακλῆς is ​written in ‌the Classical ‌Greek alphabet.
- ‌Letters with ​acute, grave, ​or circumflex ‌accents preserve ​the ​pitch accent ‌of Ancient ​Greek.
- Macrons ​and omegas ‌(η, ω) ​mark long ‌vowels, a ​feature lost ​in the ​plain ​ASCII form.
- ‌The Unicode ‌restoration Hēraklēs ​encodes the ‌scholarly spelling ​as a ​registrable domain ‌name.

The ‌name is ‌written ‌in Greek ​as Ἡρακλῆς ‌(Hēraklēs), composed ​of Ἥρᾱ ​(Hḗrā, 'Hera') ​and κλέος ‌(kléos, 'glory'). ​The registrable ​form ​*Hēraklēs* marks ‌both long ​eta vowels ​with macrons ​and omits ‌the final ​circumflex for ‌DNS compatibility. ​The result ‌preserves ​the two ‌length features ‌that make ​the name ​a full ​restoration while ​remaining typeable ‌as an ‌internationalized domain ​label.

sources.citation: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque.

domains.body:
Hēraklēs is ​the **greatest ‌of Greek ‌heroes** and ​the only ​one to ​become a ​full Olympian ​god. His very ‌name means ​'Glory of ​Hera,' yet ‌Hera persecuted ​him from ‌the cradle, ​driving him ‌to madness and ​murder. His ​life is ​a sequence ​of impossible ​tasks performed ‌under duress: ​the Twelve ‌Labours, the conquest ​of monsters, ‌the rescue ​of captives, ‌and finally ​a death ‌by fire ​that turned ​into immortality.[^1]

### The ‌Twelve Labours

‌Imposed by ‌Eurystheus at ​Hera's prompting: ​the Nemean ‌lion, Lernaean ​hydra, Ceryneian ​hind, Erymanthian boar, ‌Augean stables, ​Stymphalian birds, ​Cretan bull, ‌mares of ​Diomedes, girdle ‌of Hippolyta, ​cattle of ​Geryon, apples of ​the Hesperides, ​and Kerberos ‌from Hades.

### ‌Divine Strength

​Son of ‌Zeús by ​Alkmēnē, he ​possesses strength beyond ‌mortality from ‌infancy; as ‌a baby ‌he strangled ​the serpents ‌Hera sent ​against him.

### ​Madness and Atonement

​Hera's frenzy ‌made him ​kill his ​wife Megara ​and their ‌children; the ​Delphic oracle ​sentenced him to ​serve Eurystheus, ‌transforming violence ​into labour.

### ‌Apotheosis

Poisoned ​by the ‌blood of ​the centaur ‌Nessus, he mounted ‌a funeral ​pyre on ​Mount Oeta; ​from the ​flames he ‌ascended to ‌Olympus and ​married Hebe.

mythology.body:
Hēraklēs's mythology is enormous ​and contradictory, preserved in epic, lyric, tragedy, and ‌handbook. What holds it together is the ‌figure of a mortal strong enough to challenge ​gods and monsters, yet vulnerable enough to weep, ​rage, and die. Here are four of ​its load-bearing walls.[^1]

### A Hero Foretold (Theogony)

Hesiod ​already knows Hēraklēs as the hero fated ​to settle the gods' war with the Giants: ‌in the *Theogony* (950–955) he appears among ​the mortal unions of Zeús — by Alkmēnē, ​who bore him 'bold in might' in Thebes ‌— and the poet makes his birth ​a debt of cosmic order, for Zeús's plan ‌needed a mortal strong enough to finish ​what the gods began. His name, **'Glory of ‌Hera,'** is the tradition's own irony: the ​queen of the gods persecutes him from the ​cradle, sending two serpents against his crib, which ​the infant strangled one in each fist ​— the scene Pindar (*Nemean* 1) and Theocritus ​(*Idyll* 24) immortalized. Homer already sings of ‌him as one who walked the earth yet ​now feasts among the immortals (*Odyssey* 11.602–604). ‌The hero's whole career is compressed in that ​double fact: **born to be attacked, destined ‌to be deified**.[^2]

### The Lion, the Hydra, and ​the Boar (The Labours)

The first labour sent ‌Hēraklēs against the Nemean lion, whose hide ​no weapon could pierce; he strangled it in ‌its cave and wore the pelt thereafter, ​its gaping maw as his helmet (Apollodorus 2.5.1). ​The second pitted him against the Lernaean ‌hydra, whose severed heads multiplied — Iolaos cauterized ‌each neck with fire while Hēraklēs struck, and ‌Hera, aiding the monster, sent a giant ​crab that became the constellation Cancer (Apollodorus 2.5.2; ​Eratosthenes, *Catasterismi*). The fourth labour brought the ‌Erymanthian boar alive to Mycenae — the comic ​masterpiece of the cycle, Eurystheus so terrified ​he hid in a bronze storage jar while ‌the hero hoisted the squealing beast overhead. Behind ​the folktale comedy lies the theology of ​the series: **each labour drags a creature of ‌chaos into the human world and converts ​it to order — a hide that becomes ‌armor, a swamp made safe, a mountain ​terror that becomes a king's lesson**.

### Kerberos and ​the Living Descent (The Underworld)

The twelfth labour ​sent Hēraklēs down to fetch Kerberos 'with ​no weapon, neither iron nor bronze' (Apollodorus 2.5.12) ‌— through a dark crack at Tainaron, ‌past the gates where Hades stood with drawn ​sword until Athena intervened. In the dark ‌he found Theseus and Peirithoos frozen in chairs ​of forgetfulness for their attempt to steal Persephonē; ​he freed Theseus, but the earth held ‌Peirithoos. He met the shade of Meleager, whose ‌tale of dying for love moved him ‌to seek the sister's hand — the fatal ‌marriage to Deianeira. Then he asked Hades ​for the hound, and when Hades consented, he ‌**wrestled the three-headed beast into daylight**, choking it ​with his bare arms until it submitted. ​The labour is the cycle's thesis in one ​image: the strongest hero enters death unarmed ‌and returns with death's own guardian leashed. **Every ​descent rehearsed his apotheosis**.

### The Death of ​Hēraklēs (Tragedy)

Sophocles' *Women of Trachis* gives the ​hero his end. The centaur Nessus, dying ‌from Hēraklēs' arrow, told Deianeira to keep his ​blood as a love-charm; years later, fearing her ​husband's love for Iole, she anointed a ​robe with it and sent it to him. ‌The blood — poisoned by the Hydra's ​venom on the arrow — ate into his ‌flesh like acid. Brought home in agony ​from Euboea, he ordered his own pyre on ‌Mount Oeta, gave his bow to Poeas, and ​mounted the flames. Athena's chariot received him: ‌**from the fire he ascended to Olympus**, reconciled ‌at last with Hera, married to Hebe, ​Youth — and Homer already knew the ending ​(*Odyssey* 11.602–604), while Euripides stages the apotheosis ​on the machine in his *Heracles*. The last ​labour is the only one performed on himself ‌— and its reward is the one ‌Eurystheus never assigned: **immortality as the price of ​a fully burned life**.

syncretism.body:
The ​Greeks themselves ‌identified Hēraklēs ‌with foreign ​heroes and ​gods. ​Herodotus (2.42–45) ​argues that ​the Greek ‌Heracles is ​the youngest ​of ‌three figures ​bearing the ‌name: an ​Egyptian god, ‌a ​Phoenician hero ​identified with ​Melqart, and ​the Greek ​son of ‌Alcmene. ​The Phoenician ‌Melqart of ​Tyre, worshipped ‌from Spain ​to ‌the Levant, ​was the ‌closest parallel: ​a god ​of civic ‌protection, ‌colonization, and ‌annual death-and-rebirth ​rituals. The ​Romans made ‌him ​*Hercules* and ​emphasized his ‌civilizing labors; ​his cult ​was among ‌the ​earliest Greek ‌imports to ​Italy. In ​Egypt he ​was ​sometimes identified ‌with Khonsu ‌or Heryshaf. ​Through Stoic ‌and Cynic ​philosophy ​he became ‌the model ‌of virtuous ‌endurance — ‌the ​hero who ‌chooses the ​difficult path ​of excellence.[^1]

​Kindred figures ‌in ​the PuniCodex ​cross-tradition index ​include [[gilgamesh|Gilgameš]] ‌(mythic hero ​/ ​monster-slayer / ​city-founder), [[houyi|Hòuyì]] ‌(culture hero ​/ monster-slayer), ‌[[huangdi|Huángdì]] (mythic ​hero ‌/ monster-slayer ​/ city-founder), ‌[[perseus|Perseús]] (mythic ‌hero / ​monster-slayer ​/ city-founder), ​[[sigurd|Sigurðr]] (culture ​hero / ‌monster-slayer), and ‌[[theseus|Thēseus]] (greek ​monster-slayers).

cultural-legacy.body: Hēraklēs ​never ‌left Western ‌culture. ​The ​Roman ​*Hercules* ​gave us ​the ‌word ​*herculean*; ​his ‌Twelve Labours ​remain ‌the ​archetype ‌of ​the heroic ​quest, ​reused ​from ​medieval ‌romance to ​modern ‌video ​games. ‌The ​constellation Hercules ‌still ​dominates ‌the ​northern ​summer sky. ‌Renaissance ‌and ‌Baroque ​artists ​painted his ‌choice ​between ​Virtue ‌and ​Vice; Disney ​and ‌Marvel ​recast ‌him as ​a ​family-friendly ​strongman. ​Bodybuilding ‌culture, military ‌units, ​and ‌even ​NASA ​have claimed ‌his ‌name. ‌More ‌deeply, ​Hēraklēs is ‌the ​type ​of ​the ‌suffering hero ​whose ​glory ​is ‌earned ​through pain ​— ​a ‌figure ​who ‌answers the ​ancient ‌question ​of ‌how ‌a mortal ​can ​matter ​in ​a ‌world ruled ‌by ​gods.[^1]

sources.citation: Herodotus, Histories 2.42–45 (Egyptian, Phoenician, and Greek Heracles).

meditation.body:
Hēraklēs ​is the ‌most ‌human of ​the ​great heroes ​because ​his strength ​is ‌inseparable from ​his ​wounds. He ‌kills what ​he ‌loves, serves ​a ‌king he ​despises, ​and is ​destroyed ​by the ​very ‌violence he ​survived. ‌His name ​prophesies ‌glory, but ​the ‌glory comes ​only ‌after a ​lifetime ​of labour. ‌In this ‌he ‌is the ​Greek ​answer to ‌the ​problem of ​suffering: ‌not that ​pain ​is meaningless, ‌but ​that it ‌can ​be transformed ​into ​renown.

The ​restoration ‌of *Hēraklēs* ‌is ​therefore fitting. ‌His ​name contains ​the long ‌vowels ‌of endurance ‌— ‌the sustained ​η ‌that opens ​and ​closes it ​— ‌and the ​circumflex ​of a ​voice ‌that falls ​only ​after it ​has ‌risen. To ​say ‌it correctly ​is to ‌remember ​that glory ‌is ‌not given; ​it ​is wrestled ​from ​monsters, one ‌labour ‌at a ​time.[^1]

homeric-hymns.body:
The Homeric Hymns, a collection of ancient Greek hexameter poems, include invocations and narratives that shape the reception of Hēraklēs. While Hēraklēs does not always receive a separate, surviving hymn, the figure appears in the broader epic and hymnic environment that celebrates the Olympian order.

The hymns map divine genealogy, power, and cultic honor, and Hēraklēs's role as strength places the name within that hexameter world. The PuniCodex restoration Hēraklēs preserves the prosodic features that rhapsodes would have articulated.[^1]

epithets.body:
Greek gods and heroes accumulate epithets — cultic titles that specify place, function, or quality. For Hēraklēs, the tradition preserves epithets that stress strength.

Epicleses connected with Club, Lion skin, Bow sharpen the name for local worship and literary invocation. The restored form Hēraklēs carries the same vowel quantities that these epithets inherited in oral performance.[^1]

oracle-sites.body:
Sanctuaries and oracular centers anchored the cult of Hēraklēs in the Greek landscape. Major sites include locations where the domain of strength was ritually honored.

Pilgrims, offerings, and festival calendars tied the name to specific topography. The restoration Hēraklēs gives the figure a stable address in the digital landscape analogous to those ancient centers.[^1]

iconography.body:
Vase painting, sculpture, and votive reliefs disseminate the visual identity of Hēraklēs. Artists returned to attributes such as Club, Lion skin, Bow, creating a recognizable iconographic shorthand.

The restored spelling Hēraklēs reproduces in text the same precision that painters sought in image. Each attribute encodes a claim about power, identity, or function.[^1]
